plain: A loose sleeve of fibrous tissue around the shoulder joint. It is deliberately slack, which is what lets the shoulder move further than any other joint — and also why it dislocates so easily.
detail: Runs from the margin of the glenoid cavity to the anatomical neck of the humerus. Notably lax inferiorly, where a fold of capsule allows full abduction. Reinforced above and in front by the glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments, and all round by the rotator cuff tendons.
clinical: The capsule is weakest inferiorly, where no cuff tendon reinforces it — which is why the humeral head usually dislocates downwards and then forwards, giving an anterior dislocation. Always test the axillary nerve afterwards.

plain: A rim of fibrocartilage around the shallow shoulder socket. It deepens the socket by about half and helps hold the ball in place.
detail: A fibrocartilaginous ring attached to the margin of the glenoid cavity, deepening it and increasing the contact area with the humeral head. The long head of biceps brachii takes origin from its upper part, at the supraglenoid tubercle.
clinical: A SLAP tear runs through the superior labrum from anterior to posterior, involving the biceps anchor. A Bankart lesion is a tear of the anteroinferior labrum after anterior dislocation, and it makes recurrent dislocation much more likely.

plain: A strong band stretching from the coracoid process to the acromion. With those two bony points it forms a roof over the shoulder joint.
detail: Together with the acromion and coracoid process it forms the coraco-acromial arch, an osseoligamentous roof above the humeral head. The supraspinatus tendon and the subacromial bursa pass beneath it.
clinical: The arch prevents upward dislocation of the humeral head — but it is also what the supraspinatus tendon grinds against. Narrowing of this space causes subacromial impingement, with a painful arc between roughly 60 and 120 degrees of abduction.

plain: The strong ligament tying the collarbone down to the coracoid process. It is what actually suspends the shoulder blade from the clavicle.
detail: Two parts: the conoid ligament medially and the trapezoid ligament laterally. It is the main structure transmitting the weight of the upper limb to the clavicle.
clinical: In an acromioclavicular joint injury, a sprain of the AC ligaments alone gives a mild subluxation; once the coracoclavicular ligament also ruptures the clavicle rides high and the shoulder drops, giving the obvious step deformity.

plain: A broad band from the coracoid process to the top of the humerus, strengthening the roof of the joint capsule.
detail: Passes from the lateral border of the coracoid process to the greater and lesser tubercles, blending with the capsule and bridging the intertubercular groove.
clinical: It is the main check on inferior translation of the humeral head when the arm hangs by the side, and it thickens and contracts in adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder), which is what limits external rotation first.

plain: The small joint where the outer end of the collarbone meets the shoulder blade. You can feel it as a bump on top of the shoulder.
detail: A plane synovial joint between the lateral end of the clavicle and the acromion, often containing an incomplete fibrocartilaginous disc. It allows the scapula to rotate on the clavicle during elevation of the arm.
clinical: Injured by falling onto the point of the shoulder — a 'shoulder separation', which is quite different from a dislocated shoulder joint. Also a common site of osteoarthritis, causing pain at the top of the shoulder on cross-body adduction.

plain: The joint between the collarbone and the breastbone. It is the only true joint linking the whole upper limb to the trunk skeleton.
detail: A saddle-type synovial joint with a complete intra-articular disc, stabilised by the costoclavicular and interclavicular ligaments. It permits elevation, depression, protraction and retraction of the shoulder girdle.
clinical: Extremely strong: force applied to the shoulder fractures the clavicle long before this joint dislocates. A posterior dislocation, though rare, is an emergency because the great vessels and trachea lie directly behind it.

plain: The two short, very strong ligaments that anchor the inner end of the collarbone — one downwards to the first rib, one across to the other collarbone.
detail: The costoclavicular ligament runs from the first rib and its cartilage to the inferior surface of the medial clavicle, and is the main stabiliser of the sternoclavicular joint. The interclavicular ligament passes over the jugular notch between the two clavicles.
clinical: The costoclavicular ligament is so strong that it acts as the pivot for clavicular movement, and it is why the medial clavicle almost never dislocates — the bone breaks first.

meshNames: Long head of biceps brachii tendon.r
en: Synovial sheath of the long head of biceps
plain: The slippery sleeve wrapping the biceps tendon where it runs through the groove at the top of the humerus.
detail: A tubular extension of the synovial membrane of the glenohumeral joint that follows the tendon into the intertubercular groove. This is why the tendon is described as intracapsular but extrasynovial.
clinical: Inflammation here is bicipital tenosynovitis, giving pain localised to the front of the shoulder that is reproduced by resisted supination with the elbow flexed (Yergason's test).

plain: A flat fluid-filled sac between the roof of the shoulder and the tendon underneath it, letting the tendon glide as you lift your arm.
detail: Lies between the acromion and coraco-acromial ligament above, and the supraspinatus tendon and joint capsule below, extending laterally under deltoid. It does not normally communicate with the joint cavity.
clinical: The largest bursa in the body and a very common source of shoulder pain. If it communicates with the joint on imaging, that implies a full-thickness rotator cuff tear has connected the two.

plain: A rotator cuff muscle sitting above the spine of the shoulder blade. It starts the movement of lifting the arm sideways.
detail: From the supraspinous fossa of the scapula, passing under the acromion to the superior facet of the greater tubercle. Supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5, C6).
clinical: Initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction, after which deltoid takes over. Its tendon is the most commonly torn in the cuff, because it is squeezed in the subacromial space. Tested with the empty-can test.

plain: A rotator cuff muscle below the spine of the shoulder blade. It turns the arm outwards.
detail: From the infraspinous fossa to the middle facet of the greater tubercle. Supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5, C6).
clinical: The main lateral rotator of the shoulder. Weakness shows up as a positive external rotation lag sign, and wasting below the scapular spine is visible in suprascapular nerve entrapment.

plain: The smallest rotator cuff muscle, running from the outer edge of the shoulder blade to the back of the humerus. It also turns the arm outwards.
detail: From the upper part of the lateral border of the scapula to the inferior facet of the greater tubercle. Uniquely among the cuff, it is supplied by the axillary nerve (C5, C6).
clinical: Its axillary nerve supply means teres minor is spared in a suprascapular nerve lesion but affected in an axillary nerve injury alongside deltoid.

plain: The only rotator cuff muscle on the front of the shoulder blade. It turns the arm inwards.
detail: From the subscapular fossa on the costal surface of the scapula to the lesser tubercle of the humerus. Supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5–C7).
clinical: The sole cuff muscle inserting on the lesser tubercle, and the only medial rotator among them. Tested with the lift-off and belly-press tests. It also forms the posterior wall of the axilla.

plain: The thick triangular muscle capping the shoulder. It gives the shoulder its rounded contour and is the main muscle that raises the arm sideways.
detail: Three parts — anterior from the clavicle, middle from the acromion, posterior from the spine of the scapula — all converging on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. Supplied by the axillary nerve (C5, C6).
clinical: The middle fibres abduct from about 15 to 90 degrees. Because the axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck, a fracture there or an anterior dislocation paralyses deltoid and flattens the shoulder contour, with numbness over the regimental badge area. It is also a standard intramuscular injection site.

plain: A thick muscle from the lower outer corner of the shoulder blade to the front of the humerus. It pulls the arm down and backwards.
detail: From the inferior angle and lower lateral border of the scapula to the medial lip of the intertubercular groove. Supplied by the lower subscapular nerve (C5–C7). Not part of the rotator cuff.
clinical: Its lower border marks where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery, and it forms the lower boundary of the quadrangular and triangular spaces.

plain: The big fan-shaped chest muscle. It pulls the arm forwards and across the body.
detail: Clavicular head from the medial clavicle and sternocostal head from the sternum and upper costal cartilages, inserting by a bilaminar tendon into the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove. Supplied by the lateral and medial pectoral nerves.
clinical: Its lower border forms the anterior axillary fold. The two heads can be tested separately: the clavicular head by pushing the arm forwards, the sternocostal head by adducting against resistance.

plain: A small muscle hidden beneath pectoralis major, running from the ribs up to the coracoid process. It pulls the shoulder blade forwards and down.
detail: From the 3rd, 4th and 5th ribs to the coracoid process of the scapula. Supplied by the medial pectoral nerve.
clinical: The key landmark of the axilla: it crosses the axillary artery and divides it into three parts, and the cords of the brachial plexus are named for their position around its second part.

plain: A saw-toothed muscle spreading over the side of the ribcage. It holds the shoulder blade flat against the chest and swings it round when you raise your arm above your head.
detail: From the upper eight or nine ribs to the whole medial border of the scapula on its costal surface. Supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7).
clinical: Paralysis causes winging of the scapula — the medial border lifts off the chest wall, most obvious when pushing against a wall. It also prevents abduction beyond 90 degrees, since the scapula can no longer rotate.

plain: The large diamond-shaped muscle over the back of the neck and upper back. Its upper part shrugs the shoulders.
detail: From the external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae and the spines of C7 to T12, inserting on the lateral clavicle, acromion and scapular spine. Supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with proprioceptive fibres from C3 and C4.
clinical: Its nerve supply is a cranial nerve, not a branch of the plexus — so trapezius is tested by shrugging the shoulders when examining the accessory nerve. The nerve is superficial in the posterior triangle and vulnerable during lymph node biopsy there.

plain: The broad flat muscle of the lower back that sweeps up to the armpit. It pulls the arm down and backwards — the climbing and rowing muscle.
detail: From the thoracolumbar fascia, lower six thoracic spines, iliac crest and lower ribs, to the floor of the intertubercular groove of the humerus. Supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8).
clinical: Forms the posterior axillary fold. Remember its insertion with teres major and pectoralis major as 'a lady between two majors' — latissimus dorsi inserts into the floor of the groove, between the medial and lateral lips.

plain: Two flat muscles running downwards and outwards from the spine to the inner edge of the shoulder blade. They pull the shoulder blades together.
detail: Minor from the spines of C7 and T1, major from T2 to T5, both inserting on the medial border of the scapula. Supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C4, C5).
clinical: Retract and rotate the scapula downwards. Weakness causes a subtler winging than serratus anterior palsy, more obvious when the hands are pushed against the hips.

plain: A strap muscle from the upper neck vertebrae to the top corner of the shoulder blade. It lifts the shoulder blade.
detail: From the transverse processes of C1 to C4 to the superior angle and upper medial border of the scapula. Supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and branches from C3 and C4.

plain: The outer head of the biceps. Its tendon is unusual — it runs right through the inside of the shoulder joint before heading down the arm.
detail: Arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and the superior glenoid labrum, passes through the joint cavity inside a synovial sheath, then descends in the intertubercular groove held by the transverse humeral ligament.
clinical: It is intracapsular but extrasynovial. Because it runs through the joint it is a common source of anterior shoulder pain, and it can rupture, producing the 'Popeye sign' as the muscle belly balls up in the arm.

plain: A slim muscle from the coracoid process to the middle of the humerus. It helps pull the arm forwards and inwards.
detail: From the tip of the coracoid process, with the short head of biceps, to the middle of the medial surface of the humerus. Supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, which pierces it.
clinical: The only muscle pierced by the nerve that supplies it — a reliable way to identify the musculocutaneous nerve in the axilla.

plain: A small muscle tucked under the collarbone, running to the first rib. It steadies the clavicle during shoulder movement.
detail: From the first rib at its costochondral junction to the inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle. Supplied by the nerve to subclavius (C5, C6).
clinical: It acts as a cushion between the clavicle and the subclavian vessels beneath — so in a clavicular fracture it helps protect them from the bone ends.

plain: The prominent strap running diagonally across the side of the neck. It turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it towards its own.
detail: Sternal and clavicular heads to the mastoid process and superior nuchal line. Supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with sensory fibres from C2 and C3.
clinical: It divides the neck into the anterior and posterior triangles, the basic map for all neck anatomy. Shortening in infancy causes congenital torticollis, with the head tilted towards the affected side and turned away from it.
